title: Remainders & Modular Arithmetic
coreInsight: When division repeats in fixed groups, only the leftover position matters; numbers with the same remainder therefore behave alike for many purposes.
targetLearnerRealization: Numbers with the same remainder occupy the same repeating position after grouping, so many calculations can track only that position instead of the entire number.
learningObjectives: Write division as n = dq + r with 0 ≤ r < d.
Group integers into remainder classes and recognize that differences within a class are multiples of the modulus.
Interpret congruence as same remainder rather than ordinary equality.
Combine and filter remainder conditions while retaining the required final remainder.

continuity.openingCallback: Extend remainder zero into all possible leftover positions for a fixed divisor.
closingSeeds: Successive powers visit remainder positions in repeating cycles, so only the exponent's cycle position may matter.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: A remainder may equal or exceed the divisor.
The quotient is more important than the remainder class.
Equivalent remainder descriptions represent different modular states.

beats.purpose: Discover remainder classes as repeating positions after groups of five.
beats.expectedRealization: Numbers differing by 5 land at the same remainder position; 3, 8, and 13 all leave remainder 3.
beats.transitionIn: Divisibility marked the zero-leftover boundary. Keep walking beyond it and record every possible leftover position.
beats.transitionOut: Every five steps returned to the same position, so the quotient changed while the remainder position repeated.
beats.whyNow: A small repeating walk creates the class idea before notation.
beats.entryBridge: Group each number into complete sets of five and keep only its leftovers.
beats.exitBridge: Subtracting any two numbers in the winning set gives a multiple of five.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Five labeled remainder bins filled by a counting walk.
learnerPrompts: What remains after removing complete groups of five?
How far apart are numbers landing in the same bin?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—3, 8, and 13 all land in remainder position 3.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Divide each number by 5 and keep only the leftover amount.

visual.ariaLabel: Integers zero through fourteen sorted into five remainder bins

steps.body: Adding 5 changes the quotient by one but returns to the same leftover position.

resolution.takeaway: For a fixed divisor, remainder positions repeat every divisor steps.

beats.purpose: Establish that a valid remainder must be smaller than the divisor.
beats.expectedRealization: A leftover group of size at least d can form another complete group, so it is not a final remainder.
beats.transitionIn: A remainder is what cannot form one more complete group.
beats.prompt: Someone writes 17 = 5×2 + 7 and calls 7 the remainder. What must be fixed?

options.text: Regroup 5 of the 7 leftovers: 17 = 5×3 + 2, so the remainder is 2.
Nothing; any positive leftover is a remainder.
Change the divisor to 7.
Every remainder must be 0.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—a remainder of 7 is not final because it contains another full group of 5.
beats.incorrectFeedback: A valid remainder after division by 5 must be one of 0,1,2,3,4.

steps.body: Move one full group of 5 from the leftovers into the quotient: 5×2+7 = 5×3+2.

resolution.takeaway: When dividing by d, the remainder must satisfy 0 ≤ r < d.

beats.purpose: Characterize a remainder class by differences that are multiples of the modulus.
beats.expectedRealization: Two integers have the same remainder modulo 5 exactly when their difference is divisible by 5.
beats.transitionIn: Compare two visits to the same remainder bin without calculating either quotient.
beats.prompt: Why do 18 and 43 occupy the same remainder position after division by 5?

options.text: Their difference 43−18 = 25 is a multiple of 5.
They have the same quotient.
They have the same ones digit.
They are equal numbers.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—moving by 25 means five complete jumps of 5 and no change of remainder position.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Subtract the numbers and test the difference for divisibility by 5.

resolution.takeaway: Same remainder modulo d means the difference is a multiple of d.

beats.purpose: Separate the changing quotient from the stable remainder class.
beats.expectedRealization: Many modular questions discard complete groups and retain only the leftover position.
beats.transitionIn: The quotient records how many full laps occurred; the class records where the walk stopped.
beats.prompt: For deciding whether 18 and 43 behave the same after division by 5, which information is essential?

options.text: Their common remainder 3.
The quotients 3 and 8.
Their sum 61.
Which number is larger.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct—the quotient changes by full groups, while the remainder position controls the modular state.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Complete groups of five return to the same position and can be discarded for this question.

steps.body: Replacing 43 by 3 removes eight complete groups of 5 without changing its remainder behavior.

resolution.takeaway: Modulo a fixed divisor, complete groups fade and the remainder class remains.

beats.purpose: Introduce modular notation after same-slot meaning is secure.
beats.expectedRealization: Congruence states that two integers share a remainder for a specified modulus.
beats.transitionIn: The same-position relationship now has compact notation.
beats.name: Congruence modulo d
beats.conciseDefinition: a ≡ b (mod d) means a and b leave the same remainder when divided by d, equivalently d divides a−b.
beats.formalization: n = dq + r with 0 ≤ r < d; 43 ≡ 18 ≡ 3 (mod 5)
beats.memoryHook: Same clock position, possibly different number.

beats.expectedRealization: Congruent integers need not be equal; the modulus specifies the coarser comparison.
beats.transitionIn: The symbol resembles equality, but it compares remainder positions rather than full values.

options.text: 23 and 3 are different integers but leave the same remainder when divided by 5.
23 and 3 are ordinarily equal.
23 divided by 3 has remainder 5.
23 and 3 have the same remainder for every divisor.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—the modulus is essential, and ordinary equality is not being claimed.

steps.body: Both numbers leave remainder 3 modulo 5, yet 23 ≠ 3 as integers.

resolution.takeaway: Congruence is equality of remainder class, not equality of value.

beats.purpose: Unify positive and negative descriptions of one remainder class.
beats.expectedRealization: Remainders 4 and −1 name the same position modulo 5, though 4 is the standard remainder.
beats.transitionIn: One clock position can be described by stepping forward four or backward one.
beats.prompt: Which statement about −1 and 4 modulo 5 is correct?

options.text: −1 ≡ 4 (mod 5) because their difference is 5; the standard remainder is 4.
They represent different positions because one is negative.
−1 is the standard nonnegative remainder after division by 5.
−1 = 4 as ordinary integers.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—equivalent descriptions can name one modular state.

steps.body: Moving from −1 to 4 adds one complete cycle of 5. For standard division form, rewrite −1 as 5×(−1)+4.

resolution.takeaway: Equivalent residues differ by a multiple of the modulus; standard remainders lie from 0 to d−1.

beats.purpose: Use two remainder conditions as successive candidate filters.
beats.expectedRealization: The mod-10 condition fixes the last digit; the mod-9 condition selects 73; division by 11 leaves 7.
beats.transitionIn: A two-digit number must land in two specified remainder classes at once. Filter with the easier class first.
beats.transitionOut: Only 73 survived both conditions, and its final remainder modulo 11 is 7.
beats.whyNow: The approved problem applies same-slot reasoning as a concrete finite sieve immediately after congruence meaning is established.
beats.entryBridge: List two-digit numbers with remainder 3 modulo 10, then retain the one with remainder 1 modulo 9.
beats.exitBridge: Once the number is determined, start a fresh division by 11 and keep its remainder.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Candidate cards filtered by successive remainder conditions.
learnerPrompts: Which candidates share the required mod-10 position?
Which one also lands at remainder 1 modulo 9?
What remains after grouping that number by 11?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Numbers with remainder 3 modulo 10 end in 3; test 13,23,…,93 under the mod-9 condition.

steps.body: The remainder-3 condition modulo 10 gives candidates 13,23,33,…,93.
Only 73 satisfies 73−1 = 72 = 9×8, so N = 73.
Since 73 = 11×6+7, the requested remainder is 7.

resolution.takeaway: Multiple remainder conditions can be applied as successive filters; the quotient need not be tracked.

beats.purpose: Show that arithmetic can be performed on remainder representatives.
beats.expectedRealization: Replacing numbers by congruent small residues preserves the resulting remainder under addition and multiplication.
beats.transitionIn: Once only the remainder class matters, calculations can use small representatives.
beats.prompt: What is the remainder when 38 + 27 is divided by 5?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—38 ≡ 3 and 27 ≡ 2, so the sum is congruent to 5, whose standard remainder is 0.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Replace 38 by 3 and 27 by 2 modulo 5, then reduce the sum to 0–4.

resolution.takeaway: Add or multiply convenient representatives, then reduce to a standard remainder.

beats.purpose: Combine two aligned shortfall conditions, use an LCM connection, and compute a third remainder.
beats.expectedRealization: Adding 2 completes both groupings, so the smallest completed total is LCM(6,5)=30 and the coin count is 28, divisible by 7.
beats.transitionIn: Two remainder descriptions may hide the same shortfall from a complete group boundary.
beats.transitionOut: The shared shortfall converted both conditions into one LCM boundary; removing it gave 28 and remainder 0 modulo 7.
beats.whyNow: The approved transfer connects remainder equivalence with the earlier common-multiple structure in a nontrivial minimum problem.
beats.entryBridge: Rewrite remainder 4 modulo 6 and remainder 3 modulo 5 as being two short of a multiple.
beats.exitBridge: After finding the least coin count, divide by the new modulus 7 independently.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Remainder rows completed by the same helper coins, then aligned at an LCM.
learnerPrompts: What common shortfall do the two conditions share?
What is the first total completing both rows?
What remains when the resulting count is grouped by 7?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—the smallest count is 28, which leaves remainder 0 when divided by 7.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Add 2 to the unknown; the result must be divisible by both 6 and 5.

steps.body: Both conditions are two short of a complete group: n+2 is divisible by 6 and by 5.
The smallest positive common multiple is 30, so n = 30−2 = 28.
Since 28 = 7×4, the final remainder is 0.

resolution.takeaway: Equivalent shortfall descriptions can turn several remainder conditions into one common-multiple condition.

beats.transitionIn: Compute one standard remainder and verify its bound.
beats.transitionOut: Five is below six and cannot form another complete group.
beats.whyNow: A near item checks basic remainder calculation independently.
beats.entryBridge: Find the greatest multiple of 6 not exceeding 137.
learnerPrompts: What multiple of 6 lies just below 137?

resolution.takeaway: A standard remainder is the bounded leftover after the largest complete grouping.

beats.expectedRealization: Division by 7 permits exactly the standard remainders 0 through 6.
beats.transitionIn: Identify a value that cannot be a final leftover under grouping by seven.
beats.transitionOut: Seven leftovers would form another full group and become remainder zero.
beats.whyNow: A near item isolates the most basic remainder constraint.
beats.entryBridge: Compare each candidate with the divisor 7.
beats.exitBridge: The strict upper bound is the divisor itself.
learnerPrompts: Which candidate reaches a complete group?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—7 cannot be a remainder after division by 7.

steps.body: Possible remainders are 0,1,2,3,4,5,6. A leftover 7 becomes one more full group and remainder 0.

resolution.takeaway: The remainder is always strictly smaller than the divisor.

beats.purpose: Assess congruence via a divisible difference.
beats.expectedRealization: Fifty-eight and four differ by 54, a multiple of 9, so both have remainder 4 modulo 9.
beats.transitionIn: Recognize a shared position without computing two quotients.
beats.whyNow: A mixed item tests the structural equivalence criterion.
beats.exitBridge: A multiple-of-9 difference means no change in remainder position.

steps.body: 58−4 = 54 = 9×6, so the two integers share a remainder modulo 9. Indeed, 58 = 9×6+4.

resolution.takeaway: A divisible difference proves two integers are congruent.

beats.purpose: Assess multiplication with small remainder representatives.
beats.expectedRealization: 37×48 has the same remainder as 2×3 modulo 5, namely 1.
beats.transitionIn: Replace each factor by its small remainder before multiplying.
beats.transitionOut: The reduced product 6 returns to standard remainder 1.
beats.whyNow: A mixed item applies equivalence inside an operation.
beats.exitBridge: Reduce the product into the range 0–4.
learnerPrompts: What small residue replaces each factor?
What is the standard remainder of their product?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Compute 2×3 = 6, then remove one group of 5.

steps.body: 37×48 ≡ 2×3 = 6 ≡ 1 (mod 5). Directly, 1776 ends in 6 and leaves remainder 1 modulo 5.

resolution.takeaway: Congruent representatives may replace factors before multiplication.

beats.purpose: Assess systematic filtering under two congruence conditions and a strict bound.
beats.expectedRealization: Numbers congruent to 5 modulo 7 above 30 first meet the remainder-2 modulo-4 condition at 54.
beats.transitionIn: For the final challenge, intersect two repeating position patterns beyond a boundary.
beats.transitionOut: Testing one remainder-class list in order proves 54 is the least solution above 30.
beats.whyNow: The challenge combines class generation, filtering, and minimality.
beats.entryBridge: List numbers congruent to 5 modulo 7 above 30 and test their remainders modulo 4.
beats.exitBridge: The ordered list proves no smaller number above 30 works.
learnerPrompts: What is the first candidate above 30 in one class?
Which candidate first lands at position 2 modulo 4?
beats.incorrectFeedback: List 33,40,47,54,… from the remainder-5 class modulo 7, then test modulo 4.

steps.body: Candidates above 30 with remainder 5 modulo 7 are 33,40,47,54,… Their remainders modulo 4 are 1,0,3,2.
Therefore 54 is the first qualifying value. Check: 54 = 4×13+2 = 7×7+5.

resolution.takeaway: An ordered remainder-class list plus a second filter proves the least simultaneous solution.

beats.purpose: Consolidate bounds, class meaning, congruence, and representative arithmetic.
beats.expectedRealization: Modular reasoning tracks bounded remainder positions and treats multiples of the modulus as full cycles.
beats.transitionIn: Grouping, clocks, candidate filters, and shortfalls all use the same repeating structure.
beats.prompt: Which statements belong in reliable remainder reasoning? Select all four.

options.text: A standard remainder satisfies 0≤r<d.
Same remainder modulo d means the difference is divisible by d.
Congruence compares remainder classes, not ordinary values.
Equivalent representatives may be reduced after addition or multiplication.
Congruent numbers must have the same quotient.

response.feedback: Keep the remainder bound, divisible difference, class meaning, and reduction rules.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—those four checks capture the modular structure.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Congruent numbers may differ by many complete groups and therefore have different quotients.

resolution.takeaway: Track the remainder position; discard only complete cycles.

beats.purpose: Create the successor question about repeating units digits of powers.
beats.expectedRealization: Repeated multiplication generates a sequence of remainder positions that may cycle.
beats.transitionIn: The units digit is exactly the remainder modulo 10, so powers can be tracked on ten remainder positions.
beats.prompt: Compute the units digits of 3¹, 3², 3³, 3⁴, and 3⁵. Once a position repeats, what can the cycle tell you about a huge exponent?
beats.takeaway: Next, we will locate an exponent inside a short repeating units-digit cycle.

notes: Draft foundation lesson authored from the approved N5 compact context packet.
Repeating bins establish class meaning and the remainder bound before congruence notation.
The approved 2016 problem is the guided candidate sieve and the approved 2006 problem is the shared-shortfall transfer.
All generated answers were independently checked by quotient-remainder equations and a separate difference, enumeration, or direct-arithmetic method.
No lesson-specific renderer infrastructure was added.
